original_value: Activity-oriented cameras are increasingly being used to provide visual confirmation of specific hand-related activities in real-world settings. However, recent studies have shown that bystander privacy concerns limit participant willingness to wear a camera. Researchers have investigated different image obfuscation methods as an approach to enhance bystander privacy; however, these methods may have varying effects on the visual confirmation utility of the image, which we define as the ability of a human viewer to interpret the activity of the wearer in the image. Visual confirmation utility is needed to annotate and validate hand-related activities for several behavioral-based applications, particularly in cases where a human in the loop method is needed to label (e.g., annotating gestures that cannot be automatically detected yet). We propose a new type of obfuscation, activity-oriented partial obfuscation, as a methodological contribution to researchers interested in obtaining visual confirmation of hand-related activities in the wild. We tested the effects of this approach by collecting ten diverse and realistic video scenarios that involved the wearer performing hand-related activities while bystanders performed activities that could be of concern if recorded. Then we conducted an online experiment with 367 participants to evaluate the effect of varying degrees of obfuscation on bystander privacy and visual confirmation utility. Our results show that activity-oriented partial obfuscation (1) maintains visual confirmation of the wearer's hand-related activity, especially when an object is present in the hand, and even when extreme filters are applied, while (2) significantly reducing bystander concerns and enhancing bystander privacy. Informed by our analysis, we further discuss the impact of the filter method used in activity-oriented partial obfuscation on bystander privacy and concerns.

result.paraphrase: Activity-oriented cameras are being used more and more to visually confirm specific hand-related activities in real-world settings. Yet recent studies indicate that bystander privacy concerns reduce participants’ willingness to wear a camera. Researchers have explored various image obfuscation techniques to improve bystander privacy; however, these methods can affect the image’s visual confirmation utility differently, which we define as a human viewer’s ability to interpret the wearer’s activity in the image. Visual confirmation utility is necessary for annotating and validating hand-related activities across several behavior-based applications, especially when a human-in-the-loop approach is required for labeling, such as annotating gestures that cannot yet be detected automatically. We introduce a new form of obfuscation, activity-oriented partial obfuscation, as a methodological contribution for researchers seeking visual confirmation of hand-related activities in the wild. To evaluate it, we collected ten diverse and realistic video scenarios showing the wearer performing hand-related activities while bystanders engaged in activities that could raise concern if recorded. We then ran an online experiment with 367 participants to assess how different levels of obfuscation affected bystander privacy and visual confirmation utility. Our findings show that activity-oriented partial obfuscation (1) preserves visual confirmation of the wearer’s hand-related activity, particularly when an object is in the hand and even under extreme filters, while (2) substantially reducing bystander concerns and improving bystander privacy. Based on our analysis, we also discuss how the filter method used in activity-oriented partial obfuscation affects bystander privacy and concerns.
